name: Northern Bolivian Quechua / northern Bolivian Quechua variety of Apolo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. (Cambridge Language Surveys; ISBN 052136275X; doi:10.1017/CBO9780511486852)
catalog_locator: p. 206 (Quechua phonology, stress paragraph; page anchored by Google Books PA206; the section number 3.2.5 given by the compiler is unverified). Continuation p. 207: 'Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns.. are found in quantity-insensitive Ancash and in quantity-insensitive Cajatambo'. The book's North-Bolivian-specific passages (p. 200 Apolo; p. 357 probable, Bautista Saavedra/Muñecas) contain no stress statement.
catalog_quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junín word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable. (34) aywa-mu-ra-ygi ~ aywa-mu-ra-y [...] In the Quechua I dialects stress is maintained in word-final position when the long vowel morpheme referring to first-person subject or possessor is immediately followed by a word boundary. (Length oppositions not connected with the first-person morpheme are normally neutralised in word-final position, in which case stress is regularly assigned to the penultimate syllable.)
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

new_statements.quote: ... el acento recae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Ejemplos: lláqta pueblo 'el pueblo'; llaqta-káma pueblo-LIM 'hasta el pueblo'; llaqta-kamá-lla pueblo-LIM-DEL 'solamente hasta el pueblo'. El acento va recorriendo hacia la ... [snippet ends] (p. 223) // ... de objeto directo -ta, que muestra que en el habla muchas veces esta marca se omite, quedando como huella simplemente la acentuación de la palabra en la última sílaba. (p. 270)
new_statements.translation: ... the accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Examples: lláqta 'the town'; llaqta-káma 'as far as the town'; llaqta-kamá-lla 'only as far as the town'. The accent keeps moving toward the ... (p. 223) // ... the direct-object marker -ta, which shows that in speech this marker is very often omitted, leaving as its only trace the accentuation of the word on the last syllable. (p. 270)
new_statements.citation: Plaza Martínez, Pedro. 2009. Quechua. In Mily Crevels & Pieter Muysken (eds.), Lenguas de Bolivia, tomo I: Ámbito andino, 215-284. La Paz: Plural editores.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (Google Books search-within-volume, id 26LdarGBj0UC = Crevels & Muysken eds. 2009 Lenguas de Bolivia I) holds one hit, page_id PA223: ".. recae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Ejemplos : lláqta pueblo llaqta - káma pueblo - LIM ' el pueblo ' ' hasta el pueblo ' llaqta - kamá - lla pueblo - LIM - DEL ' solamente hasta el pueblo ' El acento va recorriendo hacia la.."; and the copied all-volume file give the same PA223 snippet with the preceding words "el acento recae en la penúltima..". the compiler quote is this text with the interlinear table re-linearised (gloss lines moved next to each example) and hyphen spacing normalised; wording identical. p.270…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the whole word including suffixes; each added suffix moves the stress one syllable to the right (lláqta > llaqta-káma > llaqta-kamá-lla). The stress is therefore predictable and non-contrastive. Same rule stated for Kallawaya 'as in Quechua' (Muysken 2009:154) and for Quechua generally (Adelaar & Muysken 2004:206).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (search-within-volume for 'acento secundario' returns no hit in the volume).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 270: colloquial omission of accusative -ta leaves final-syllable stress as its trace (i.e. surface final stress on such words). Adelaar & Muysken 2004:206 add, for Quechua generally, that interjections and emphatic expressions can have word-final stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (grammatical word with suffixes); citation forms. The chapter describes Bolivian Quechua in general (in practice the Cochabamba/Chuquisaca norm), not the North La Paz variety specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: No opened source describes stress for North Bolivian Quechua (Apolo / Charazani, norte de La Paz; ISO qul, nort2976) itself. The quoted statement (Plaza Martínez 2009:223) is from the 'Quechua' chapter of Lenguas de Bolivia I, which describes Bolivian Quechua in general and which Glottolog files under South Bolivian Quechua [quh] (sout2991); search-within-volume shows the chapter never mentions Apolo or Charazani. The same penultimate rule is stated first-hand for Kallawaya (ISO caw), the mixed language of Charazani whose grammar is the local North Bolivian Quechua (Muysken 2009:154, 'como en quechua'), and for Quechua generally by Adelaar & Muysken 2004:206. The qul-specific descriptions (Stark 1972b 'Notes on the Quechua of Apolo'; Stark 1985; Kronemeijer to appear 'Sketch Grammar of Charazani Quechua') could not be opened or appear silent on stress. Glottolog's own 15 refs for nort2976 are mostly misfiled Cuzco Quechua items.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (penultimate) as the existing statement from Plaza Martínez 2009 (p. 223, 'el acento recae en la penúltima sílaba'), but only as a family-wide generalisation ('most Quechua dialects') that covers North Bolivian Quechua by default; the book contains no stress statement specific to the Apolo/Charazani variety (queries 'Bolivian Quechua' AND 'stress', 'Callahuaya' AND 'stress'/'penultimate'/'accent' return nothing relevant). It adds the interjection/emphatic word-final exception, which the catalog quote does not have. Opened only via archive.org full-text-search snippets: the WALS open_url is a bibliographic record with no text, the CUP DOI page is login-only, and the archive.or…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level rule: in most Quechua dialects stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word form (so stress marks word edges). The named exceptions (word-final stress in interjections/emphatic expressions; final-syllable elision in Tarma and northern Junín; retained final stress on the first-person long vowel in Quechua I; initial or weight-dependent stress in quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo, p. 207) are all Peruvian and none concerns Bolivian Quechua. The book's own passages on the northern Bolivian variety (p. 200: Apolo, Franz Tamayo, keeps syllable-final stops and has glottalised/aspirated stops per Stark 1985b; p. 357 probable: the Bautista Saavedra and Muñecas variety 'defined as Northern Bolivian Quechua in Stark (1985b)', closer to Cuzco/Puno Quechua than to mainstream Bolivian Quechua) say nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the recovered passages.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alalaw 'how cold!'); word-final stress from final-syllable elision in Tarma and northern Junín Quechua; word-final stress on the first-person long-vowel morpheme in Quechua I dialects; word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent stress in quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo (p. 207). None is attributed to Bolivian Quechua.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken describe North Bolivian Quechua only in passing: p. 184 Map 5 lists 'Northern Bolivian (Apolo)' under Quechua IIC; p. 200 cites Stark (1985b) on the Apolo variety (province of Franz Tamayo, La Paz); p. 357 (probable) describes the Quechua of the provinces of Bautista Saavedra and Muñecas (Charazani area, base of Callahuaya) as 'Northern Bolivian Quechua in Stark (1985b)', closer to Cuzco and Puno Quechua than to mainstream Bolivian Quechua. The stress rule quoted is the general Quechua rule (sec. 3.2.5), not a description of this lect. The existing Plaza Martínez 2009 statement is from a chapter Glottolog files under South Bolivian Quechua (sout2991), so the catalog still has no first-hand stress statement for nort2976.
